message.content:
The lion (*Panthera leo*) and the zebra (*Equus quagga*) are both mammals, but they belong to very different branches of the mammalian tree:

| Taxonomic level | Lion | Zebra |
|-----------------|------|-------|
| Kingdom | Animalia | Animalia |
| Phylum | Chordata | Chordata |
| Class | Mammalia | Mammalia |
| Infraclass | Eutheria (placentals) | Eutheria (placentals) |
| Order | Carnivora | Perissodactyla |
| Family | Felidae | Equidae |
| Genus | Panthera | Equus |
| Species | *Panthera leo* | *Equus quagga* |

Because they diverged early in mammalian evolution, their most recent common ancestor (MRCA) is a fairly ancient mammal that lived well before the split between the carnivoran and perissodactyl lineages. Current molecular phylogenies place this MRCA at roughly 100–120 million years ago, during the late Cretaceous period. This ancestor would have been a small, generalized placental mammal—often referred to as a “stem‑placental” or “basal eutherian”—that possessed the basic mammalian toolkit (e.g., differentiated teeth, a three‑bone middle ear, and a relatively high metabolic rate).

In short, the common ancestor of lions and zebras is a basal placental mammal that lived about 100–120 million years ago, long before the diversification of the modern orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla.
